prompt.context_jp: 富士山のふもとに広がる富士浅田___、二月の澄んだ光をやわらかく受けていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富士浅田___、二月の澄んだ光をやわらかく受けていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that frames the town as the chapter's topic.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is setting the scene by presenting Fuji-Asada as the known theme we'll follow — exactly what は does at the start of a scene-setting paragraph.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the town as brand-new information in a bare announcement ('There was Fuji-Asada…'), which doesn't fit this calm, descriptive opening.

contrast_examples.jp: 富士浅田は静かな町だ。
contrast_examples.en: Fuji-Asada is a quiet town. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: あっ、富士浅田が見えた。
contrast_examples.en: Oh, Fuji-Asada just came into view. (new info)

prompt.context_jp: 若い制作担当が持ち込んだ企画に、上司の視線___すっと薄く曇る。
prompt.prompt_jp: 上司の視線___すっと薄く曇る。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that reports the newly-observed change in gaze.

feedback.correct_en: This is a freshly observed event — the gaze clouding over at this moment. が marks that spontaneous, new-information observation.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn the gaze into an already-established topic, which clashes with the sudden perceptual shift the sentence is reporting.

contrast_examples.en: His gaze clouded over. (observed event)
His gaze (as for it) was cold. (describing a known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 上司の眉___わずかに動いたのを、彼は見逃さなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 上司の眉___わずかに動いたのを、彼は見逃さなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle inside the subordinate clause describing the small movement.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a 〜のを embedded clause reporting a one-time observed event, Japanese defaults to が. The eyebrow movement is the fresh detail he notices.
feedback.incorrect_en: は almost never appears as the subject of a 〜のを subordinate clause describing a single observed action; it would wrongly make the eyebrow the main topic.

contrast_examples.en: I saw that he smiled.
He smiled. I was watching. (two separate main clauses)

prompt.context_jp: 支配人的にはＯＫだったんスけど オーナーからＮＧ___出たらしくて
prompt.prompt_jp: オーナーからＮＧ___出たらしくて
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that marks what newly came out of the owner.

feedback.correct_en: NGが出る is a fixed pattern reporting a new rejection coming down. が introduces the NG as the fresh piece of news.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn 'NG' into an already-known topic, which doesn't fit here — it's the whole point of the news.

contrast_examples.en: Permission came through. (new info)
As for permission, it won't come. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 二月の朝___まだ冷たく、指先が痺れるほど、頬にはひどく痛い風が触れていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 二月の朝___まだ冷たく、…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that sets 'February morning' as the paragraph's topic.

feedback.correct_en: This sentence makes a general characterization of the February morning as the scene's theme. は is the natural topic marker for that framing.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like reporting a specific instant ('A February morning was still cold!'), not setting a scene the rest of the paragraph will develop.

contrast_examples.en: Mornings are cold. (general topic)
Morning came. (new event)

prompt.context_jp: 運転手___前回ホテルまで客を運んだ男で、彼らの顔をよく覚えていたのだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 運転手___前回ホテルまで客を運んだ男で、…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle introducing 'the driver' as the topic being described.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence is an identification/description of the driver — 'The driver was the same man who…'. は fits the X は Y だ identification frame.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make this sound like fresh event-reporting, not the explanatory 'this driver was that same person' identification the narration intends.

contrast_examples.en: He is a doctor. (identification)
A doctor came. (event)

prompt.context_jp: このホテル___、外から見ればけっして華やかではない。
prompt.prompt_jp: このホテル___、外から見ればけっして華やかではない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that sets up an implicit contrast ('on the outside… but inside…').

feedback.correct_en: The narration is setting up a 'not glamorous outside, but has its own charm' contrast across the next sentences. は naturally signals that contrastive framing.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would simply announce the hotel as new, losing the 'yes, but…' feel that the paragraph then develops.

contrast_examples.jp: 外は寒いが、中は暖かい。
contrast_examples.en: Outside is cold, but inside is warm. (contrast)
It's cold outside. (plain report)

prompt.context_jp: レジ打ち___速い おばちゃんがいるんです
prompt.prompt_jp: レジ打ち___速い おばちゃんがいるんです
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle inside the relative clause 'the cashier whose scanning is fast'.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a relative clause modifying おばちゃん, the subject of 速い naturally takes が. The whole clause 'レジ打ちが速い' describes the lady.
feedback.incorrect_en: は almost never appears as the subject inside a relative clause — it would try to set 'register scanning' as the main topic of the whole sentence, which doesn't work here.

contrast_examples.en: a person who is tall (relative clause)
That person is tall. (main clause: は for topic, が for attribute)

prompt.context_jp: フロントの空気___ふっと変わり、清美は顔を上げて自動ドアの向こうに目をやった。
prompt.prompt_jp: フロントの空気___ふっと変わり、…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that reports the sudden sensed change.

feedback.correct_en: A momentary, newly-noticed shift in the atmosphere is classic new-information が territory.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 'the atmosphere' sound like an ongoing theme being contrasted, missing the suddenness that triggers Kiyomi to look up.

contrast_examples.en: A wind blew. (fresh event)
The wind is cold. (describing the known wind)

prompt.context_jp: 若葉___父親と久しぶりの外出を楽しんでいて、昼食のあとの少し眠たいような会話が続いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 若葉___父親と久しぶりの外出を楽しんでいて、…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that sets Wakaba as the paragraph topic.

feedback.correct_en: The paragraph shifts focus to Wakaba and describes her ongoing afternoon. は sets her up as the known topic to be elaborated on.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight Wakaba as new/exhaustive ('It's Wakaba who…'), which doesn't match the gentle narrative transition here.

contrast_examples.en: Wakaba laughed. (topic continuation)
It was Wakaba who laughed. (identifying who)

prompt.context_jp: ほかに 泊まりたい所があったけど 部屋___取れなかったからなのかなと思って
prompt.prompt_jp: 部屋___取れなかったからなのかなと思って
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that fits inside 'because a room couldn't be booked'.

feedback.correct_en: In '〜が取れなかった' (couldn't get a room/ticket), the thing you failed to secure is marked with が in this subordinate reason clause. It's the inability-to-obtain pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would wrongly turn 'the room' into a contrasted topic ('as for the room, it wasn't taken…'), losing the natural 'couldn't book one' meaning.

contrast_examples.en: I couldn't get a ticket.
As for tickets, I did get them. (contrasting with something else)

prompt.context_jp: 由美___面白がるような視線を隣に向け、次の一言を待っている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 由美___面白がるような視線を隣に向け、…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that keeps Yumi as the ongoing topic.

feedback.correct_en: Yumi has just been mentioned; this sentence continues the two-person scene by shifting the camera to her side. は is the topic-continuation marker.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would awkwardly re-introduce Yumi as if she were a brand-new participant, which conflicts with the preceding counter-talk.

contrast_examples.en: She smiled. (continuing)
She came in. (newly entering the scene)

prompt.context_jp: 岸本___持ち出した名前は、想定していたのとは違うものだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 岸本___持ち出した名前は、想定していたのとは違うものだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for Kishimoto inside the relative clause.

feedback.correct_en: '岸本〜持ち出した名前' is a relative clause modifying 名前. The subject inside a relative clause takes が. The main-clause topic marker は already appears later on 名前.
feedback.incorrect_en: You can't have two は in parallel here; using は for Kishimoto would compete with 名前は and break the sentence structure.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が言った言葉は忘れられない。
contrast_examples.en: The words he said are unforgettable.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は忘れられない言葉を言った。
contrast_examples.en: He said unforgettable words. (he = main topic)

prompt.context_jp: ホテルのすぐ外に岸本と松崎の姿___あった。
prompt.prompt_jp: ホテルのすぐ外に岸本と松崎の姿___あった。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for the existential 'there was…'.

feedback.correct_en: This is a classic existence/presentation sentence ('…の姿があった') introducing where the characters now are. が is required with ある in this presentational pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn 'their figures' into a known topic being contrasted, which doesn't fit the scene-setting flow.

contrast_examples.en: There was a cat there. (presentation)
The cat was there (as for it).

prompt.context_jp: 高速移動するメガネの男性を 見たって人___何人かいて
prompt.prompt_jp: 高速移動するメガネの男性を 見たって人___何人かいて
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for 'several people exist who said…'.

feedback.correct_en: '〜人が何人かいて' is existence: introducing some new people whose existence the producer is reporting. が marks that newly-introduced subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would already presuppose these witnesses as known, but the whole point is to bring them up for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: そう言う人が何人かいた。
contrast_examples.en: There were several people who said so. (new info)

contrast_examples.jp: その人は何人か知っている。
contrast_examples.en: As for those people, I know a few. (known topic)

prompt.context_jp: これまで 古きよき町として 親しまれてきた富士浅田___ですが…
prompt.prompt_jp: 親しまれてきた富士浅田___ですが…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that signals the 'but…' turn is coming.

feedback.correct_en: The newscaster is contrasting Fuji-Asada's past image with a 'but today…' twist. は both sets the topic and signals that contrast is coming after ですが.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just announce the town bluntly as new info, missing the 'has always been X, but now…' setup that the clause with ですが is building.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は普段は優しいですが…
contrast_examples.en: He's usually kind, but… (contrast)
He is the kind one. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 逆に ウチのバスマット___ 薄くて かったいじゃないですか
prompt.prompt_jp: 逆に ウチのバスマット___ 薄くて かったいじゃないですか
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that explicitly contrasts their mats with the big hotels' fluffy ones.

feedback.correct_en: The word 逆に ('on the other hand') makes this a direct contrast with the big-chain mats. は is the natural contrastive-topic marker here.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read as introducing the mats as new info, losing the explicit 'ours, by contrast…' meaning that 逆に is setting up.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は背が高いが、弟は低い。
contrast_examples.en: He's tall, but his brother is short. (contrast)
The younger brother is short. (plain)

prompt.context_jp: お客さん さっき ___って言ってましたけど ___ますよ
prompt.prompt_jp: さっき ___って言ってましたけど ___ますよ
prompt.prompt_en: The driver teases them: 'you said you were ___, but you're actually ___'. Pick the right expression.

choices.text: ツイてない / ツいて
付いてない / 付いて

feedback.correct_en: ツイてない/ツいてる is the idiomatic '(un)lucky' expression — exactly what the driver flips on them when he turns up with new info.
feedback.incorrect_en: 疲れない doesn't fit the fortune/luck meaning; 付いている in that spelling means 'be attached', not 'be lucky', and loses the idiomatic nuance.

contrast_examples.en: I'm lucky today.
I'm having zero luck.

prompt.context_jp: “いちやま”に レジ打ちが 超速い人がいるって話をしたのね… そしたら あの人 結構 ___ててさ
prompt.prompt_jp: あの人 結構 ___ててさ
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the verb that means 'took the bait / got really interested'.

feedback.correct_en: 食いつく (literally 'bite into') is the idiomatic way to describe someone eagerly latching onto a story — perfect for the producer's reaction.
feedback.incorrect_en: 飲み込む means to swallow/comprehend, and 振り向く is to turn around — neither conveys 'got hooked on the topic'.

contrast_examples.en: He bit into / jumped on that story.

contrast_examples.jp: ようやく話を飲み込んだ。
contrast_examples.en: He finally grasped the story.

prompt.context_jp: “敷地の外なら いいですか？”って聞かれてさ — 「___」
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi reacts to the TV crew's persistence. Pick the best fit.

feedback.correct_en: しぶとい captures 'tenacious, won't give up' — exactly what Kiyomi says about the crew finding a workaround after being told no.
feedback.incorrect_en: やさしい ('kind') and のんびり ('laid-back') describe the opposite temperament and would make no sense as a reaction to their pushiness.

contrast_examples.en: That's a persistent salesman.
He's a laid-back person.

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺さん 今日いるといいですね — 「まあ いたら ___ よな」
prompt.prompt_jp: まあ いたら ___ よな
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the set phrase meaning 'things will go quickly / be easy'.

feedback.correct_en: 話が早い (often written 話は早い when topicalized) is the idiom for 'then it'll be quick/straightforward' — perfect for 'if he's there, this is easy'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 話が長い means 'long-winded' — the opposite feel; 話を切る means to cut off a conversation, which doesn't fit this hopeful 'if so, easy' line.

contrast_examples.jp: 本人がいれば話は早い。
contrast_examples.en: If the person himself is there, it'll be quick.
That person is long-winded.

prompt.context_jp: 「なるほど ___ね」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「なるほど ___ね」
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the natural phrase for 'that's a shame / what a waste'.

feedback.correct_en: もったいない expresses regret that something good is being wasted — the senior producer's reaction to a juicy clip going unused.
feedback.incorrect_en: うらやましい ('envious') and ありがたい ('grateful') don't match 'the hotel won't let us use it' — nothing here is enviable or thankful.

contrast_examples.jp: 使わないのはもったいない。
contrast_examples.en: It's a waste not to use it.
I'm grateful for the help.

prompt.context_jp: 上村さま ___ この度は 合格 おめでとうございます
prompt.prompt_jp: 上村さま ___
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the hotel-staff greeting for a returning expected guest.

choices.text: お待ちしておりました

feedback.correct_en: お待ちしておりました is the humble-polite set phrase hotel staff use to greet an awaited guest — matches the front-desk register perfectly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 待っていました is plain polite and too flat for service speech; 待ってたよ is casual and inappropriate from staff to a guest.

contrast_examples.jp: お待ちしておりました。
contrast_examples.en: We've been expecting you. (service keigo)
I've been waiting for you! (casual among friends)

prompt.context_jp: だから バスタオルと___ 体拭いちゃうこと ありません？
prompt.prompt_jp: バスタオルと___ 体拭いちゃうこと
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the verb that means 'mistake it for' a bath towel.

feedback.correct_en: 〜と間違って is the common 'mistaking X for Y' pattern — exactly the mix-up Yumi is describing.
feedback.incorrect_en: 違って means 'differing from', and 変わって means 'changing'; neither expresses the mistaken-identity nuance.

contrast_examples.en: I mixed up salt and sugar.
Salt and sugar are different.

prompt.context_jp: Senior producer's suggestion to a junior crew member about where to film.
prompt.prompt_en: Which casual advice sounds most natural coming from a senior to a junior in this scene?

choices.text: ホテルの近くで張っといて 外でインタビューすればさ ホテルには 迷惑は かからないんじゃない？
ホテルの近くに張ることで、外でインタビューをすることにすれば、ホテルに迷惑はかからないのではないでしょうか？
ホテル近所張って外インタビュー、迷惑ない。

feedback.correct_en: Option A is the real-feel senior-to-junior pitch: casual 〜といて, 〜すればさ, 〜んじゃない？ — chatty but still guiding.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is grammatical but stiff/formal, sounding more like a written proposal; C is telegraphic and ungrammatical, missing particles and verb forms.

contrast_examples.jp: 外でやればいいんじゃない？
contrast_examples.en: Why not just do it outside? (casual suggestion)

contrast_examples.jp: 外で行うのが望ましいと思われます。
contrast_examples.en: It is thought desirable to do it outside. (formal/written)

prompt.context_jp: Front-desk staff thanking a returning guest.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural from hotel staff to a returning guest?

choices.text: いえいえ こちらこそ また ご利用いただき ありがとうございます
いえいえ こちらこそ また 使ってくれて ありがとう
こちらこそ ご利用になってくださいまして ありがとうございました

feedback.correct_en: A is standard service keigo: ご利用いただき is the humble construction naturally paired with ありがとうございます to a guest.
feedback.incorrect_en: B drops into casual speech (使ってくれて, ありがとう) which is wrong for front-desk register. C mixes ご利用になる (respectful) with くださいまして awkwardly and sounds overdone/garbled.

contrast_examples.jp: ご利用いただきありがとうございます。
contrast_examples.en: Thank you for using our service. (natural keigo)

contrast_examples.jp: 使ってくれてありがとう。
contrast_examples.en: Thanks for using it. (casual, wrong register)

prompt.context_jp: Kiyomi teasing Yumi's weak selling point for the hotel.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds like natural teasing between coworkers?

choices.text: “ここにしかない よさ”で 1コ目が“味”って だいぶ弱くない？
“ここにしかない よさ”で 1つ目は“味”ということですが、少々弱いのではないでしょうか？
“ここにしかない よさ”で 1コ目“味”、弱い。

feedback.correct_en: A has the casual counter 1コ目, the colloquial って quotation, and 弱くない？ tag — the exact register two coworkers tease each other in.
feedback.incorrect_en: B shifts into formal written register that doesn't fit a counter-side chat; C drops too many particles and the quotation marker, sounding like notes rather than speech.

contrast_examples.en: 'Character' as your #1 is kinda weak, right? (natural banter)

contrast_examples.jp: 一つ目が味というのは弱いでしょうか。
contrast_examples.en: Would 'character' as the first point be weak? (formal/stiff)

prompt.context_jp: Yumi describing what makes the job feel rewarding.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds like natural spoken Japanese for 'that makes me happy'?

choices.text: “ありがとうね”とか 言ってくれたり また来てくれたりしたら うれしいじゃないですか
“ありがとうね”などと 言ってくださり また来てくださる場合は 嬉しく感じます
“ありがとうね”って言ったり来たりは、うれしい。

feedback.correct_en: A uses natural 〜たり〜たりしたら and the sympathy-seeking 〜じゃないですか tag — the real conversational pattern Yumi uses with her senior.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is overly formal/written (などと, 場合は, 感じます) and sounds like a report. C compresses so much that the particles and listing structure break down.

contrast_examples.jp: 来てくれたりしたら嬉しいじゃないですか。
contrast_examples.en: If they come back, that's nice, right? (natural)

contrast_examples.jp: お越しいただいた際には嬉しく存じます。
contrast_examples.en: I would be pleased on the occasion of their visit. (formal)

prompt.context_jp: The senior producer sensing something odd is going on in town.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version best captures a journalist's hunch 'this isn't ordinary'?

choices.text: 周りが やけに かばってる感じとか見ると… ちょっと ただ事じゃない感じしない？
周りの人々が異常に庇護している様子を鑑みますと、尋常ではないという印象を抱かざるを得ません。
周りかばってる見て ただごとない？

feedback.correct_en: A uses やけに, 〜感じとか見ると, and 〜感じしない？ — the natural half-musing, half-asking register of a producer thinking out loud.
feedback.incorrect_en: B shifts into dense written/formal Japanese (鑑みますと, 抱かざるを得ません) that nobody would say aloud on a stakeout; C drops particles and verbs to the point of being broken speech.

contrast_examples.jp: なんか、ただ事じゃない感じしない？
contrast_examples.en: Doesn't it feel kinda unusual? (spoken hunch)

contrast_examples.jp: 尋常ではない事態と推察されます。
contrast_examples.en: The situation is inferred to be extraordinary. (written report)
